content: DOCK8, also known as Dedicator of Cytokinesis 8 or Zir3, is a large intracellular protein with a molecular weight of approximately 190 kDa. It plays a critical role in intracellular signaling pathways. This protein belongs to the DOCK-C subfamily of the DOCK family of guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs), which are responsible for activating small G proteins. DOCK8 was initially discovered through a yeast two-hybrid (YTH) screen aimed at identifying proteins that interact with the Rho family small G protein Cdc42. Subsequent northern blot analysis revealed that DOCK8 is highly expressed in the placenta, lung, kidney, and pancreas, with lower expression levels observed in the heart, brain, and skeletal muscle. Structurally, DOCK8 shares the same core domain arrangement as other DOCK proteins. It contains a DHR2 domain, which in other proteins is associated with GEF activity, and a DHR1 domain, which is known to interact with phospholipids. In the YTH system, DOCK8 was reported to interact with both Rac1 and Cdc42. However, stable interactions between DOCK8 and these small G proteins were not observed in GST-pulldown assays. This lack of stable interaction may be due to the requirement of adaptor proteins to stabilize the complex and facilitate nucleotide exchange, as seen in many DOCK-G protein interactions. Mutations in the DOCK8 gene are associated with the autosomal recessive form of Job's syndrome, also known as hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES). This condition typically manifests in infancy, with affected individuals surviving into late childhood or adolescence. The disease is characterized by eczema, recurrent cold staphylococcal abscesses, recurrent lung infections, coarse facial features (thickened skin), retention of primary teeth (resulting in two rows of teeth), elevated IgE levels, and eosinophilia. Although the cellular role of DOCK8 is not fully understood, its importance has been highlighted in studies showing that disruption of the DOCK8 gene is implicated in disease. Deletion or reduced expression of DOCK8 has been reported in human lung cancer cell lines, and DOCK8 has been identified as a potential candidate gene associated with glioma progression. Autosomal recessive DOCK8 deficiency is linked to a variant of combined immunodeficiency, specifically a form of hyperimmunoglobulinemia E syndrome (HIES). This clinical entity, first described in 2004, is caused by biallelic germline mutations in the DOCK8 gene. DOCK8 deficiency presents with distinct clinical features compared to other forms of HIES and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Clinical manifestations include recurrent infections, allergies, and malignancies. Nearly all patients experience recurrent or chronic upper and lower respiratory tract infections, often requiring sinus surgery and myringotomy tube placement. Recurrent lung infections can lead to bronchiectasis, a condition characterized by widened and scarred airways. Skin infections in DOCK8 deficiency are notable and include severe and difficult-to-treat viral infections such as herpes simplex virus, human papillomavirus, and molluscum contagiosum; bacterial infections such as Staphylococcus aureus; and fungal infections of the mouth or skin caused by Candida. Eczema is common and can be severe, often complicated by bacterial infections. These skin infections can become disfiguring. Patients with DOCK8 deficiency frequently have allergies to various food and environmental allergens, as well as asthma. Autoimmune manifestations, such as autoimmune hemolytic anemia, vasculitis, and vasculopathy, have also been observed. Additionally, patients are at increased risk for developing squamous cell carcinomas and lymphoid malignancies. Some lymphomas are associated with poor control of the Epstein–Barr virus, a cancer-causing virus. These cancer risks are significant, and patients should be closely monitored for signs of malignancy. DOCK8 deficiency is classified as a combined immunodeficiency because it involves both reduced lymphocyte numbers and defective lymphocyte function. It can also be categorized as a type of autosomal recessive hyperimmunoglobulinemia E syndrome. Laboratory findings include progressive lymphopenia, primarily affecting CD4 and CD8 T cell subsets, as well as reduced B cell and/or NK cell counts in some patients. Eosinophilia and immunoglobulin abnormalities are also common. Antibody responses to vaccines are frequently poor. Loss of DOCK8 protein expression can be demonstrated through diagnostic intracellular flow cytometry testing. Once a diagnosis is established, treatment is tailored to the individual’s clinical condition and may include medications and other strategies to manage infections, allergies, and asthma. Supportive care often involves prophylactic antimicrobials and consideration of immune globulin replacement. Interferon-alpha has been used to control severe viral infections, such as widespread warts or herpes simplex virus. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative in many primary immunodeficiencies and has been successfully used in patients with DOCK8 deficiency.
